vignette:
The boy who became a principal at twenty-two had learned early that adults could not be predicted. Marcus’s childhood home in a small Liberian town had been a place where the sound of his father’s footsteps on the wooden porch meant a switch or a belt or a closed fist, but never a hug. The beatings came without warning, triggered by a half-eaten bowl of rice or a question asked at the wrong moment. His mother worked two jobs and was rarely there to intervene. By the time Marcus was ten, he had learned to read the air, to gauge the tilt of a man’s shoulders, to know when to disappear. But no amount of vigilance ever stopped the unpredictability. That was the terror at the core of it: the certainty that he could do everything right and still be hurt.

Now, at twenty-two, Marcus ran a small charter school in a Midwestern city. He had escaped Liberia with an aunt at fourteen, earned a scholarship, and worked his way through college in four years. He had a girlfriend, a quiet apartment, a job that mattered. But the old memories were never far. They came as fragments—disconnected pieces that refused to form a coherent story. When he tried to deliberately remember what had happened, the details slipped away, like trying to hold water in his hands. Then, without warning, a photograph from his childhood would surface on his phone—his aunt had sent a scanned image of him at age seven, standing rigid beside a man whose face he could not look at—and the memory would crash over him with a force that made the present moment dissolve. The memory felt more real than ordinary life. The linoleum floor of his office, the hum of the fluorescent lights, the stack of files on his desk: all of it became thin and insubstantial compared to the smell of kerosene and dust, the weight of his own small body braced for impact.

The nightmares were worse. He would wake gasping, the residue of the dream clinging to him like smoke. In the dream, he was always a child again, and his father was standing over him, but the room was wrong—it was his own bedroom here in America, or the school hallway, or a place he did not recognize. The disorientation lasted for hours. His girlfriend, who slept beside him, had learned not to touch him when he woke. The first time she had reached for him, he had thrown himself out of bed, heart hammering, certain for a moment that she was part of the threat.

Marcus had come to believe that he had permanently changed for the worse. The boy he had been—the one who could laugh, who had wanted to be a teacher—felt like a stranger. What remained was a man who was terrified of his own anger. He had never hit anyone. He had never even raised his voice in a professional setting. But he was certain that if he ever let the rage inside him out, he would do something terrible. So he clamped down on every flash of irritation, every moment of frustration, until his jaw ached and his shoulders were knotted with tension. When a student talked back, Marcus smiled tightly and walked away. When a teacher missed a deadline, he wrote a polite email instead of calling a meeting. He could not risk it. He could not stop bad things from happening to him—that lesson was carved into his bones—but he could try to be so small, so careful, so controlled, that nothing bad would ever have a reason to come near him again.

The unpredictability of daily life was a constant minefield. A sudden loud noise in the hallway—a door slamming, a stack of books falling—made him flinch so violently that students had started to notice. He had begun arriving at school an hour early, just to have the building empty and quiet. He had stopped attending faculty meetings where the agenda was not distributed in advance. He had started avoiding the hallway near the boiler room, because the clanking pipes sounded too much like footsteps on a wooden porch.

What finally brought Marcus to seek help was a morning in late October. He had woken from a nightmare, and when his girlfriend asked him what was wrong, he had opened his mouth and found that he could not speak. The words were there, but they would not come out. He had sat on the edge of the bed, trembling, while she held his hand and said nothing. That silence, her patience, was what broke something open inside him. He was afraid—deeply, viscerally afraid—that if he started talking about what had happened, he would never stop, and that the rage he had spent fifteen years containing would finally, inevitably, escape. But he was also, for the first time in a very long time, hoping that he might be wrong.
